Guidance for AI coding agents working with this repository.

Fizzy is a kanban-style project management and issue tracker: cards move across columns on boards, with comments, mentions, and assignments.

## Deploy

Default branch: `main`

Self-hosted deploys run Kamal against `config/deploy.yml` — see `docs/kamal-deployment.md`.

## SaaS mode

For local agent work, `tmp/saas.txt` is the checkout-level SaaS switch used by `bin/setup`. When present, read `saas/AGENTS.md` before continuing. Otherwise, do not apply its instructions.

## Architecture Overview

### Multi-Tenancy (URL-Based)

Fizzy uses **URL path-based multi-tenancy**:
- Accounts have a unique decimal `external_account_id` used in URL prefixes
- URLs are prefixed: `/{account_id}/boards/...`
- Middleware (`AccountSlug::Extractor`) extracts the account ID from the URL and sets `Current.account`
- The slug is moved from `PATH_INFO` to `SCRIPT_NAME`, making Rails think it's "mounted" at that path
- Tenant-scoped domain records are account-isolated; global identity, session, and authentication records are exceptions
- Background jobs automatically serialize and restore account context

**Key insight**: This architecture allows multi-tenancy without subdomains or separate databases, making local development and testing simpler.

### Authentication & Authorization

Passwordless magic link authentication. A global `Identity` (email-based) can have `Users` in multiple Accounts, so an email is not a single account membership. Users have roles: owner, admin, member, system. Board-level access control via `Access` records.

### Entropy System

Cards automatically "postpone" (move to "not now") after inactivity:
- Account-level default entropy period
- Board-level entropy override
- Prevents endless todo lists from accumulating
- Configurable via Account/Board settings

### UUID Primary Keys

All tables use UUIDs (UUIDv7 format, base36-encoded as 25-char strings):
- Custom fixture UUID generation maintains deterministic ordering for tests
- Fixtures are always "older" than runtime records
- `.first`/`.last` work correctly in tests

### Background Jobs (Solid Queue)

Database-backed job queue (no Redis):
- Custom `FizzyActiveJobExtensions` prepended to ActiveJob
- Jobs automatically capture/restore `Current.account`
- Mission Control::Jobs for monitoring

Recurring tasks are declared in `config/recurring.yml`.

### Sharded Full-Text Search

Full-text search runs in the database, not Elasticsearch. On MySQL it is sharded 16 ways by CRC32 of the account ID (`Search::Record::Trilogy`); on SQLite it is a single FTS5 index (`Search::Record::SQLite`). Don't assume the sharded shape when working under SQLite. Models in `app/models/search/`.

### Imports and exports

Allow people to move between OSS and SAAS Fizzy instances:
- Exports/Imports can be written to/read from local or S3 storage depending on the config of the instance (both must be supported)
- Must be able to handle very large ZIP files (500+GB)
- Models in `app/models/account/data_transfer/`, `app/models/zip_file`

## Conditional returns

```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.
3. `private` methods

## Invocation order

We order methods vertically based on their invocation order. This helps us to understand the flow of the code.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    method_1
    method_2
  end

  private
    def method_1
      method_1_1
      method_1_2
    end
  
    def method_1_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_1_2
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2
      method_2_1
      method_2_2
    end
  
    def method_2_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

## To bang or not to bang

Should I call a method `do_something` or `do_something!`?

As a general rule, we only use `!` for methods that have a correspondent counterpart without `!`. In particular, we don’t use `!` to flag destructive actions. There are plenty of destructive methods in Ruby and Rails that do not end with `!`.

## Visibility modifiers

We don't add a newline under visibility modifiers, and we indent the content under them.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    # ...
  end

  private
    def some_private_method_1
      # ...
    end

    def some_private_method_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

**Deep Dive into Drag-and-Drop Implementation**

Okay, I need to get this straight. The task is to make card dragging feel instant, with no visual shifting after the drop. I've got to analyze how the app works for moving cards and what effects are visible and/or trigger visual changes on the board. So, first I'll re-read the prompt and make sure I understand the requirements completely. It's all about smooth transitions and no janky shifts once the drag is complete, like the prompt says: "no waiting on the save, nothing shifting afterwards."

I'll start by breaking down each column type (`Not Now`, `Maybe?`, Board Columns, `Done`) to understand how cards are ordered, and what happens when they get moved.

**1. `Not Now`:** When a card is "postponed," the `last_active_at` is updated. Since these cards are sorted using `latest`, the card will automatically move to the top of the column. This means when a card is dropped into the 'Not Now' column, any server-side changes would immediately move the newly added card to the top, causing the very shifting behavior the prompt wants us to avoid.

**2. `Maybe?`:** For "awaiting triage" cards, the `latest` ordering is modified by the `with_golden_first` scope, ensuring golden cards are positioned at the top of the list. When a card is sent back to triage, and the `last_active_at` is updated, the card will become the first item (if golden) or go right after the golden cards (if it isn't golden). Again, this can cause a shift.

**3. Board Columns:** This is similar to `Maybe?`. I've got `active` cards, then `latest` combined with the `with_golden_first` scope. When a card is triaged into a column, a `last_active_at` timestamp is updated, causing either a jump to the top (if golden), or move to after golden cards (if it isn't golden). This means that on drop there is a potential visual "shift" that the prompt is telling me to avoid.

**4. `Done`:** With "closed" cards, the order uses `recently_closed_first`, which orders by `closures.created_at`. When a card is closed, the `closure` is created and `created_at` timestamped. This means that a newly "closed" card goes to the top. This will also cause a janky shift during the drop.

I'm starting to see a pattern here. The way we're currently ordering cards means the server-side update will cause cards to "shift" after the drop (the opposite of what the prompt wants).

Now I'm going to look more closely at the prompt. It specifies: "Columns keep their own order—dragging moves a card between places, not within one." And importantly, the "Dragging only feels right when it's instant." So I need to ensure that when a card is dropped, the change is *visually* instant *without* any server-side order changes visibly shifting the card.

So, how do I achieve "no shifting afterwards?"

Here are the key aspects of the design:

**Optimistic UI:** When the user drops a card, *immediately* update the DOM with the card in its new position. This optimistic approach makes the drag-and-drop feel instant.

**Background Saving:** The server should handle the database update in the background.

Now I need to think about what this *really* means. Suppose I move a card from `Column A` to `Column B`.

1.  **Card Position in Target Column:**
    If I *naively* just stick the dragged card at the top, when the server-side updates come through, it'll jump around. This violates the prompt! So I need to factor in card sorting from the database to avoid this.

So what about card appearance?

2.  **Card Appearance/Classes/Visuals:** What is different between these columns, and how does the styling need to change (visually) so it looks right?

This is where I'll need to examine the CSS and the associated HTML/Ruby files.

I need to make sure:
*   I *immediately* update the card's styling and classes on the optimistic update.
*   I make sure the card's visual state on drop reflects its new column or status.

So, I'll examine the files related to those visual changes.

**Analyzing the Implications of Optimistic DOM Updates with Turbo Streams**

Okay, so here's the deal. I'm focusing on how we handle card drops, specifically the trade-offs between how we send the HTTP request and update the DOM. I'm zeroing in on two key approaches:

**Option 1:** Optimistically update the DOM immediately on `drop`, and then send the request with `responseKind: "turbo-stream"`. The server responds with `turbo_stream.replace(..., method: :morph, ...)` – which will involve a `turbo-frame.reload()`.

**Option 2:** Still optimistically updating the DOM on `drop`, but sending a request with `responseKind: "json"` (or "turbo-stream" but *without* the morph).

I need to nail down the specifics of **Option 1**, tracing every little detail. Let's see what happens when the `turbo_stream.replace` command with `:morph` is executed on the server. I'm looking at `create.turbo_stream.erb` files, which include `turbo_stream.replace` directives, and also the partials being replaced.

It's all about how these `turbo_stream.replace` calls function within the context of the `<turbo-frame>` structure. **Optimizing Drag-and-Drop in Fizzy: A Deep Dive**

Okay, here's what I'm thinking. The development database isn't migrated, but the test database is. That's good to know. And it seems that with `RAILS_ENV=test`, we're already using `with_automatic_pagination` where needed which is great because this is already accounted for in `cards_controller_test.rb` and `boards_controller_test.rb`.

My focus now is the choice between `"json"` and `"turbo-stream"` for `responseKind`. The core issue, as the prompt states is: "Dragging only feels right when it's instant: when you let go, the board is already the way you left it — no waiting on the save, nothing shifting afterwards."

The critical point here is to avoid anything shifting after the drop. I see two potential failure modes. The first is waiting for the server, which is unacceptable. The second is the DOM update after the server update.

Let's break down using `turbo-stream`. If the save finishes, and triggers a `turbo-stream` morph or reload, we have several issues. The current page has to have a `<turbo-frame>`. If we did a `turbo-stream` `morph` or `reload` and, for example, rendered an empty turbo frame, that extra `GET` request just gets sent. If we use `turbo-stream`, what happens if there are entropy bubbles, or "last updated" info, or even a second drag happening while the save is finishing? The current drag is disrupted. If the column is scrolled, a reload can jump the scroll position and cards disappear.

Okay, let's look at the alternative. If we avoid `turbo-stream` and go with a purely optimistic update, we can eliminate the "waiting on the save" and "shifting afterwards" problems, because the card placement is immediately reflected in the DOM at drop. It's the "nothing shifting afterwards" that is the issue with `turbo-stream`.

Now, let's assess the implications of `responseKind: "json"`. Specifically, it seems our existing controllers (`Cards::TriagesController`, `Cards::ClosuresController`, and `Cards::NotNowsController`) have existing `format.json { head :no_content }` which is perfect. Checking all the existing actions in these controllers, they all have a `:no_content` response for JSON requests. Furthermore, the test in `test/controllers/cards/triages_controller_test.rb:23` is very instructive. `delete card_triage_path(card), as: :turbo_stream` redirects the Turbo stream request.

Wait, looking at `form_helpers.js`, the use of `responseKind: "json"` with `@rails/request.js` is intentional for background persistence because the client DOM *already* has the desired state. With `responseKind: "json"` and `X-Turbo-Request-Id`, the current tab won't morph or reload and other tabs will be updated via broadcast, which means NO shift afterwards!

So, can this be validated? Can an optimistic DOM update be made 100% faithful to a fresh page render? When the board is updated, nothing will shift, no matter what happens, since the board is updated locally!

### Part 3: Drag & Drop: Event Handling, Hover Highlighting

Let's dissect HTML5 Drag and Drop events and ensure we're prepared for every edge case.

1.  **Nested `dragenter` / `dragleave` Flicker Bug:** This is a classic. As a pointer enters a child element within a container, `dragenter` and `dragleave` fire in a nested fashion. If not handled carefully, this can lead to the column highlight flickering on and off, which is unacceptable. My solution: Track the current container (`this.#currentContainer`) or check the `event.relatedTarget`. When a `dragover(event)` occurs:
    *   First, confirm we have a dragged item ( `this.#draggedItem`).
    *   Then, find the target container using `event.target.closest('[data-drag-and-drop-target~="container"]')`.
    *   Now, here's where we get smart: we need to handle the source column carefully. "Dragging moves a card between places, not within one". Design has provided the styles, so the column under the pointer lights up, and the dragged card dims. We've got to carefully consider whether the column the card is dragged from should be highlighted. If it is, the UX tells the user "you can drop it here in the same column!" - this is false, as we don't support moving cards within the same column.
    *   I've determined that the source column should *not* light up. This ensures the user isn't misled. Also, if we don't call `event.preventDefault()` on `dragover` over the source column, Chrome displays a "no-drop" cursor and, upon release, may render a distracting "snap-back" animation. Calling `preventDefault()` avoids all this, giving a smooth UX.

    *   `dragleave` should carefully evaluate `event.relatedTarget` to determine when to clear the highlight: only clear the highlight if we are leaving a container.

    *   Similarly, `drop`, `dragend`, and `disconnect` should also ensure that no stale highlights are ever left on elements.

2.  **`dragstart` Details:** Only elements with `[data-drag-and-drop-target~="item"]` are draggable. If dragging an item, verify we're not in a mobile viewport (or prevent the event). I'll set `event.dataTransfer` appropriately: `effectAllowed = "move"` and `setData("text/plain", item.id)` and add the class that dims the card (synchronously).
    *   A synchronous class addition on `dragstart` has no race condition and is completely deterministic. We'll add `.drag-and-drop__dragged-item` *synchronously* to dim the card and capture the correct drag ghost image.

3.  **Click vs. Drag on a Card:** It's essential to understand the click behavior of cards. A card uses a link (`<a>`) that covers the whole card. If the user clicks (mousedown + mouseup without dragging) on the card, the link fires, and Turbo navigates. However, if they press and drag, the drag takes precedence because the `<a>` inside the card has `draggable="false"`. If an element inside a `card` (such as an image or link inside a card) does not have `draggable="false"`, the user may trigger a drag event on the wrong element! We need to verify that we've correctly assigned `draggable="false"` on elements that shouldn't be draggable.

With these fine-grained details addressed, the drag-and-drop experience will be seamless.

steps.reasoning_content:
**A Chromium Bug! A Big One!**

Whoa, hold up! Look at this output! `DEBUG events=["mousedown:A#","dragstart:ARTICLE#...", "dragend:ARTICLE#...", "click:A#"]` This is massive! We've just uncovered a real-world Chromium bug that's pretty significant.

Here's the scenario: Chromium, when dealing with a `translate` transition, is firing a `click` event *immediately* after a `dragend` event when the drag started and ended on the same element. It's happening because, during the animation of the `translate` transition, the element under the mouse pointer changes, and both `mousedown` and `mouseup` land on the same `<a class="card__link">` after a drag event. This causes Chromium to fire a `click` event *right after* `dragend`, which is definitely not the expected behavior.

Think about a user's experience: they grab a card to drag it, change their mind, and drop it back where they started. Boom, the browser unexpectedly navigates to the card's page! Super annoying, right?

The fix is surprisingly simple: In `drag_and_drop_controller.js`, we can introduce a flag, `this.#justDragged = true`, when `dragStart` fires. Then, when `dragEnd` fires, we can set up a mechanism to suppress the next `click` event. We'll listen for `click` events in the capture phase (or using a custom event and listener on the `.card-columns` element) and, if a click arrives immediately after `dragend`, we'll prevent it. The key is suppressing the click only in the *same turn* (or browser input task) after dragend!

Crucially, this won't affect regular clicks because `dragstart` and `dragend` aren't involved in a normal click. Also, since Chrome fires the click *immediately* after `dragend`, we can suppress that click by simply setting the `this.#justDragged = true` flag and clearing it on the next task (with `setTimeout(..., 0)`). This is a clean and effective way to block the unexpected click events after a drag.

This single fix for `--seed 13583` addresses a genuine Chromium UX bug that would affect a real user cancelling a drag on the same card. I'm going to add `#suppressNextClick` to `drag_and_drop_controller.js` immediately! This will run in capture phase on `this.element`, *before* any other click handlers.

steps.message:
I have implemented drag-and-drop for moving cards between columns and statuses on the board:

- **Stimulus controller (`app/javascript/controllers/drag_and_drop_controller.js`)**:
  - Enables HTML5 dragging on card items within `.card-columns` on desktop viewports (`(min-width: 640px)`) and preserves `draggable` attributes across Turbo morphs and frame renders.
  - Applies `.drag-and-drop__dragged-item` to dim the dragged card and `.drag-and-drop__hover-container` to highlight target columns under the pointer (ignoring the card's current column and preventing child-element `dragleave` flicker).
  - Ignores drops on the card's current column so columns keep their own order and dragging only moves cards between places.
  - Performs optimistic DOM updates synchronously on `drop`—inserting the card in its destination column's natural order (after golden cards for `Maybe?` and board columns, or at the top for `Not Now` and `Done`), updating card classes/colors/metadata, revealing/hiding empty-column placeholders, and adjusting column counts—while persisting the change asynchronously via JSON (`FetchRequest`) so nothing shifts after the save completes.
- **Board & Card Views / Helpers (`app/helpers/columns_helper.rb`, `app/views/boards/**`, `app/views/cards/display/_preview.html.erb`, `app/javascript/controllers/navigable_list_controller.js`)**:
  - Wired `drag-and-drop` controller, targets, classes, drop URLs (`triage`, `not_now`, `closure`), card status/color metadata, and unconditional empty placeholders so CSS `:has(.card)` transitions empty states immediately on drop.
- **System Tests (`test/system/drag_and_drop_test.rb`)**:
  - Added end-to-end system tests covering column/status transitions, collapsed and expanded drop targets, column ordering (including golden cards and same-column no-ops), instant optimistic updates with delayed saves and zero post-save layout shift, visual drag/hover styles, normal card clicks, and post-morph dragging.
